title: A challenging year as some super funds go backwards
full_text:
The nation’s best-performing super funds earned double-digit returns over the past year, while the worst funds fared so badly they put members in negative territory.
One of the nation’s biggest super funds, the $100bn industry fund Hesta, returned just 3.3 per cent in its sustainable growth fund over the 12 months to June 30.
That’s lower than the cash rate, which hovered between 3.6 per cent and 4.35 per cent over the year, and is also below inflation of about 4 per cent.
In dollar terms, a 3.3 per cent return means someone with $150,000 in their super account at the start of the financial year would have increased it by less than $5000 by the end of the year, excluding contributions.
A bad year can be smoothed out over time: across 10 years, Hesta’s sustainable growth option has returned 8 per cent a year on average.
But staying in a fund that frequently underperforms has major consequences down the line. Over five years, Hesta’s sustainable fund has returned just 4.5 per cent a year.
Taking the above example of a $150,000 super balance and a 3.3 per cent annual return, a worker on an average salary of $100,000 would finish the year with a $165,000 balance, excluding tax. That’s with the 12 per cent super guarantee doing the heavy lifting.
If that return is repeated over another two years, the balance by the end of year three is $197,000, again excluding fees. The total gain is close to $50,000, but investment returns would have contributed only about $16,000 of that.
Taking the same starting balance and salary, with a 9 per cent return, the total at the end of year three would sit at just under $228,000, excluding fees.
That’s a $30,000 difference over only three years. The gap would grow much larger over time.
While Hesta’s sustainable option was by far the biggest underperformer among the majors, its default MySuper option, where most of its members are invested, was around the median at 9.5 per cent.
A Hesta spokeswoman said the sustainable growth option’s underperformance was affected by its US tech stock positioning.
The sustainable option also lacked exposure to energy and resources stocks, which went on a tear over the past 12 months, driven by Middle East conflicts and a commodities boom.
“We understand sustainable growth’s financial-year-to-date return will be a disappointing result for members invested in this option,” the spokeswoman said.
“Sustainable growth faced broader headwinds with international active equity managers generally adopting lower exposure to major US technology stocks. Considerable challenges have also emerged for the US renewables sector, including higher interest rates, import tariffs and policy uncertainty.” Given current geopolitical uncertainty and backlash against “green” and ESG initiatives over the past 18 months, chances are those challenges will hang around for some time yet.
This probably means a dampened outlook for green funds, and it could test ethical investors’ convictions on ESG investing.
Hesta has broadened the sustainable option’s investment universe this year, probably in response to the underperformance.
“We are continuing to refine the strategy of this investment option, and through the year have increased diversification within sustainable growth to help manage risk and improve resilience across market conditions,” the fund said.
Hesta’s green option was the worst of the lot among the megafunds, but outside the majors other ethical funds also underperformed.
Australian Ethical’s Australian shares option couldn’t even get into positive territory, returning negative 6 per cent for the 12 months to June 30.
Westpac, NAB, CSL, Macquarie and New Zealand’s Contact Energy were the option’s top five holdings, with Macquarie the only one to make any decent gains over the year.
CSL shares fell more than 50 per cent over the year, wiping out about $60bn from its market cap.
The local sharemarket significantly underperformed global counterparts over the past 12 months, but still returned about 6 per cent, inclusive of dividends.
Australian Ethical’s balanced and growth optionsreturned 6 per cent and 6.5 per cent respectively.
Sustainable options at other funds, including AustralianSuper, Australian Retirement Trust, Aware, Hostplus and Rest, managed to avoid a similar fate this year, returning in the range of 8-9 per cent for members.
